summary: This standards-track RFC defines a hierarchical way of encoding Join/Prune attributes in PIM messages, more efficient when the same attribute values apply to many sources. It updates RFC 5384 by renaming the encoding type registry there.

eli5.summary: Instead of repeating the same label on every item, you write it once for the whole group.

questions: what is pim hierarchical join prune
how do pim join attributes override each other
subtitle: Write a PIM Join/Prune attribute once for a whole message or group instead of repeating it for every source.

tldr.problem: In a PIM Join/Prune message, attributes had to be specified separately for each joined or pruned source, even when many sources needed the same attribute and value.
tldr.mechanism: Attributes can also be encoded in the Upstream Neighbor Address (applying to every source in the message) and in a Group Address (applying to every source in that group set). The most specific level wins when the same attribute appears at several levels.
tldr.outcome: The meaning of attributes does not change; only the encoding gets more compact. Routers advertise support with a new Hello Option, type 36.

today: RFC 7887 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It updates RFC 5384 by renaming the encoding type registry.

sections.title: The Repetition Problem
sections.content:
RFC 5384 lets a PIM Join/Prune message carry a set of attributes for each joined or pruned source. Each source needs its own copy, even when the same attributes and values apply to some or all of the sources in the message.

RFC 7887 adds a hierarchical encoding. If the same attribute and value applies to all sources, it is specified once in the message. If it applies to all sources in one group set, it is specified once for that group set.

The document also notes that what RFC 5384 calls Join attributes also apply to pruned sources, so it uses the more accurate name Join/Prune attributes.
sections.eli5: Saying the same thing over and over for every item is wasteful. This RFC lets you say it once for everything it covers.

sections.title: Three Levels of Attributes
sections.content:
A Join/Prune message has a single Upstream Neighbor Address and one or more group sets. Each group set has a Group Address plus a list of Joined Sources and a list of Pruned Sources. These are encoded in Encoded-Unicast, Encoded-Group and Encoded-Source format, as defined in RFC 7761.

RFC 7887 builds a hierarchy on top of these fields:

  • Attributes in the Upstream Neighbor Address apply to every source in the message. This is the least specific level.
  • Attributes in a Group Address apply to every source in that group set.
  • Attributes in a source address apply to that single source, as in RFC 5384.

This works because the encoding type from RFC 5384 is extended to the Encoded-Unicast and Encoded-Group formats as well.
sections.eli5: There is a rule for the whole school, a rule for each class, and a rule for one kid. Each kid follows all three.

sections.title: Combining and Overriding Attributes
sections.content:
The full set of attributes for a source is built by combining the message-wide attributes, the attributes of its group set, and its own source-specific attributes. If the same attribute appears at more than one level, the most specific level overrides the others.

The set is formed before any attribute is processed. So a value that is invalid for its type can still override a valid value from a higher level.

The RFC gives an example. A source has T_1=V_1, T_2=V_2 and T_3=V_3. Its group address carries T_1=V_6 and T_4=V_4. The upstream neighbor address carries T_1=V_7, T_4=V_8 and T_5=V_5. The result is T_1=V_1, T_2=V_2, T_3=V_3, T_4=V_4 and T_5=V_5.

This document does not change the meaning of any attribute. Encoding all the attributes in the source address would give exactly the same meaning.
sections.eli5: If the school says wear a hat but your class says no hats, you follow the class rule. The most specific rule wins.

sections.title: PIM Address Encoding Types
sections.content:
PIM addresses carry an address family and an encoding type. This applies to Encoded-Unicast, Encoded-Group and Encoded-Source addresses, and the type says how the address is encoded whatever the address type.

As currently defined, type 0 is native encoding (RFC 7761) and type 1 is Join/Prune attributes encoding (RFC 5384). A type 1 encoded address MUST contain at least one Join/Prune attribute.

The RFC notes that future encoding types might not apply to all address types.
sections.eli5: Each address has a small tag saying how it is written. Tag 0 means plain, and tag 1 means plain plus extra labels.

sections.title: The Hierarchical Join/Prune Attribute Hello Option
sections.content:
A PIM router announces support by putting the Hierarchical Join/Prune Attribute Hello Option in its PIM Hello messages. The option has OptionType = 36 and OptionLength = 0, so it carries no value. A router that includes it MUST also include the Join Attribute Hello Option from RFC 5384.

A router MUST NOT send a Join/Prune message with attributes in the Upstream Neighbor Address or any group address out of an interface that has a PIM neighbor that has not included this option in its Hellos.

The reason is that even a router that is not the upstream neighbor must parse the message, in order to perform Join suppression and Prune override.
sections.eli5: Before using the shortcut, a router checks that all its neighbors say they understand it. Otherwise some would be confused.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says that using the encoding has no impact on security beyond using the RFC 5384 encoding. A forged message with certain attribute values is equally hard to make with either encoding. A wrong message-wide attribute can affect all sources in the message, but without this encoding the same wrong attribute would be repeated for every source and have the same effect.

IANA renamed the registry "PIM Encoded-Source Address Encoding Type Field" to "PIM Address Encoding Types", with the same content. It also added Hierarchical Join/Prune Attribute (36) to the "PIM-Hello Options" registry.
sections.eli5: Writing a label once does not make it easier to trick anyone than writing it many times. The registry just got a clearer name.
